hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to **bright, elongated linear structures**—typically **diagonal bands, rods, or specular highlights**—set against a **dark, low-contrast background**. The activating feature is consistently a **luminous white, silver, or pale gray** strip, often resulting from a longitudinal reflection on a cylindrical object (such as a metal rod, pen, or pipe) or a sharp illuminated edge, oriented diagonally (most commonly descending from upper-left to lower-right). The background is typically **dark grey, charcoal, or black**, creating a stark high-contrast polarity with the foreground element. The feature typically traverses the frame, occupying approximately **10–30% of the image width** while spanning the majority of its diagonal length. The neuron remains invariant to the object's identity (e.g., hardware, stationery, organic forms) and surface material, provided the **strong light-on-dark contrast** and **diagonal linear form** are maintained.
